entries.d63b9d3c6132f07a84bda43f2b92f61275d9a45d: <div sID="gen26109" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="16" osisID="Luke.16" sID="Luke.16"/> <div eID="gen26109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26110" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen26111" type="x-p"/> The scope of Christ's discourse in this chapter is to awaken and quicken us all so to use this world as not to abuse it, so to manage all our possessions and enjoyments here as that they may make for us, and may not make against us in the other world; for they will do either the one or the other, according as we use them now. I. If we do good with them, and lay out what we have in works of piety and charity, we shall reap the benefit of it in the world to come; and this he shows in the parable of the unjust steward, who made so good a hand of his lord's goods that, when he was turned out of his stewardship, he had a comfortable subsistence to betake himself to. The parable itself we have (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.1-Luke.16.8">ver. 1-8</reference>); the explanation and application of it (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.9-Luke.16.13">ver. 9-13</reference>); and the contempt which the Pharisees put upon the doctrine Christ preached to them, for which he sharply reproved them, adding some other weighty sayings, <reference osisRef="Luke.16.14-Luke.16.18">ver. 14-18</reference>. II. It, instead of doing good with our worldly enjoyments, we make them the food and fuel of our lusts, of our luxury and sensuality, and deny relief to the poor, we shall certainly perish eternally, and the things of this world, which were thus abused, will but add to our misery and torment. This he shows in the other parable of the rich man and Lazarus, which has likewise a further intention, and that is, to awaken us all to take the warning given us by the written word, and not to expect immediate messages from the other world, <reference osisRef="Luke.16.19-Luke.16.31">ver. 19-31</reference>.
entries.536cd4996b60f546006923ce9b7faed86065d6c7: <div eID="gen26111" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen26110" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Unjust Steward.</title> <div sID="gen26112" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And he said also unto his disciples, There was a certain rich man, which had a steward; and the same was accused unto him that he had wasted his goods. <hi type="super">2</hi> And he called him, and said unto him, How is it that I hear this of thee? give an account of thy stewardship; for thou mayest be no longer steward. 3 Then the steward said within himself, What shall I do? for my lord taketh away from me the stewardship: I cannot dig; to beg I am ashamed. <hi type="super">4</hi> I am resolved what to do, that, when I am put out of the stewardship, they may receive me into their houses. 5 So he called every one of his lord's debtors <hi type="italic">unto him,</hi> and said unto the first, How much owest thou unto my lord? 6 And he said, A hundred measures of oil. And he said unto him, Take thy bill, and sit down quickly, and write fifty. <hi type="super">7</hi> Then said he to another, And how much owest thou? And he said, A hundred measures of wheat. And he said unto him, Take thy bill, and write fourscore. <hi type="super">8</hi> And the lord commended the unjust steward, because he had done wisely: for the children of this world are in their generation wiser than the children of light. <hi type="super">9</hi> And I say unto you, Make to yourselves friends of the mammon of unrighteousness; that, when ye fail, they may receive you into everlasting habitations. <hi type="super">10</hi> He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much. <hi type="super">11</hi> If therefore ye have not been faithful in the unrighteous mammon, who will commit to your trust the true <hi type="italic">riches?</hi> <hi type="super">12</hi> And if ye have not been faithful in that which is another man's, who shall give you that which is your own? <hi type="super">13</hi> No servant can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon. <hi type="super">14</hi> And the Pharisees also, who were covetous, heard all these things: and they derided him. <hi type="super">15</hi> And he said unto them, Ye are they which justify yourselves before men; but God knoweth your hearts: for that which is highly esteemed among men is abomination in the sight of God. <hi type="super">16</hi> The law and the prophets <hi type="italic">were</hi> until John: since that time the kingdom of God is preached, and every man presseth into it. <hi type="super">17</hi> And it is easier for heaven and earth to pass, than one tittle of the law to fail. <hi type="super">18</hi> Whosoever putteth away his wife, and marrieth another, committeth adultery: and whosoever marrieth her that is put away from <hi type="italic">her</hi> husband committeth adultery. <div eID="gen26112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26113" type="x-p"/> We mistake if we imagine that the design of Christ's doctrine and holy religion was either to amuse us with notions of divine mysteries or to entertain us with notions of divine mercies. No, the divine revelation of both these in the gospel is intended to engage and quicken us to the practice of Christian duties, and, as much as any one thing, to the duty of beneficence and doing good to those who stand in need of any thing that either we have or can do for them. This our Saviour is here pressing us to, by reminding us that we are but <hi type="italic">stewards of the manifold grace of God;</hi> and since we have in divers instances been unfaithful, and have forfeited the favour of our Lord, it is our wisdom to think how we may, some other way, make what we have in the world turn to a good account. Parables must not be forced beyond their primary intention, and therefore we must not hence infer that any one can befriend us if we lie under the displeasure of our Lord, but that, in the general, we must so lay out what we have in works of piety and charity as that we may meet it again with comfort on the other side death and the grave. If we would act wisely, we must be diligent and industrious to employ our riches in the acts of piety and charity, in order to promote our future and eternal welfare, as worldly men are in laying them out to the greatest temporal profit, in making to themselves friends with them, and securing other secular interests. So <hi type="italic">Dr. Clarke.</hi> Now let us consider, <div eID="gen26113" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26114" type="x-p"/> I. The parable itself, in which all the children of men are represented as <hi type="italic">stewards</hi> of what they have in this world, and we are but stewards. Whatever we have, the property of it is God's; we have only the use of it, and that according to the direction of our great Lord, and for his honour. Rabbi Kimchi, quoted by Dr. Lightfoot, says, "This world is a house; heaven the roof; the stars the lights; the earth, with its fruits, a table spread; the Master of the house is the holy and blessed God; man is the steward, into whose hands the goods of this house are delivered; if he behave himself well, he shall find favour in the eyes of his Lord; if not, he shall be turned out of his stewardship." Now, <div eID="gen26114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26115" type="x-p"/> 1. Here is the <hi type="italic">dishonesty</hi> of this <hi type="italic">steward.</hi> He <hi type="italic">wasted his lord's goods,</hi> embezzled them, misapplied them, or through carelessness suffered them to be lost and damaged; and for this he was <hi type="italic">accused to his lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.16.1">v. 1</reference>. We are all <hi type="italic">liable</hi> to the same charge. We have not made a due improvement of what God has entrusted us with in this world, but have perverted his purpose; and, that we may not be for this <hi type="italic">judged of our Lord,</hi> it concerns us to <hi type="italic">judge ourselves.</hi> <div eID="gen26115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26116" type="x-p"/> 2. His <hi type="italic">discharge</hi> out of his place. His lord <hi type="italic">called for him,</hi> and said, "<hi type="italic">How is it that I hear this of thee?</hi> I expected better things from thee." He speaks as one sorry to find himself disappointed in him, and under a necessity of dismissing him from his service: it troubles him to hear it; but the steward cannot deny it, and therefore there is no remedy, he must make up his accounts; and be gone in a little time, <reference osisRef="Luke.16.2">v. 2</reference>. Now this is designed to teach us, (1.) That we must all of us shortly be discharged from <hi type="italic">our stewardship</hi> in this world; we must not always enjoy those things which we now enjoy. Death will come, and <hi type="italic">dismiss</hi> us from our stewardship, will <hi type="italic">deprive</hi> us of the abilities and opportunities we now have of doing good, and others will come in our places and have the same. (2.) That our discharge from our stewardship at death is <hi type="italic">just,</hi> and what we have deserved, for we have wasted our Lord's goods, and thereby forfeited our trust, so that we cannot complain of any wrong done us. (3.) That when our stewardship is taken from us we must <hi type="italic">give an account</hi> of it to our Lord: <hi type="italic">After death the judgment.</hi> We are fairly warned both of our discharge and our account, and ought to be frequently thinking of them. <div eID="gen26116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26117" type="x-p"/> 3. His <hi type="italic">after-wisdom.</hi> Now he began to consider, <hi type="italic">What shall I do?</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.16.3">v. 3</reference>. He would have done well to have considered this before he had so foolishly thrown himself out of a good place by his unfaithfulness; but it is better to <hi type="italic">consider</hi> late than never. Note, Since we have all received notice that we must shortly be turned out of our stewardship, we are concerned to consider what we shall do then. He must live; which way shall he have a livelihood? (1.) He knows that he has not such a degree of industry in him as to get his living by work: "<hi type="italic">I cannot dig;</hi> I cannot earn by bread by my labour." But why can he not dig? It does not appear that he is either old or lame; but the truth is, he is <hi type="italic">lazy.</hi> His <hi type="italic">cannot</hi> is a <hi type="italic">will not;</hi> it is not a natural but a moral disability that he labours under; if his master, when he turned him out of the stewardship, had continued him in his service as a labourer, and set a task-master over him, he would have made him dig. He <hi type="italic">cannot dig,</hi> for he was never used to it. Now this intimates that we cannot get a livelihood for our souls by any labour for this world, nor indeed do any thing to purpose for our souls by any ability of our own. (2.) He knows that he has not such a degree of <hi type="italic">humility</hi> as to get his bread by begging: To <hi type="italic">beg I am ashamed.</hi> This was the language of his pride, as the former of his slothfulness. Those whom God, in his providence, has disabled to help themselves, should not be <hi type="italic">ashamed</hi> to ask relief of others. This steward had more reason to be ashamed of cheating his master than of begging his bread. (3.) He therefore determines to make friends of his lord's debtors, or his tenants that were behind with their rent, and had given notes under their hands for it: "<hi type="italic">I am resolved what to do,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.16.4">v. 4</reference>. My lord turns me out of his house. I have none of my own to go to. I am acquainted with my lord's tenants, have done them many a good turn, and now I will do them one more, which will so oblige them that they will bid me welcome to their houses, and the best entertainment they afford; and so long as I live, at least till I can better dispose of myself, I will quarter upon them, and go from one good house to another." Now the way he would take to make them his friends was by striking off a considerable part of their debt to his lord, and giving it in his accounts so much less than it was. Accordingly, he sent for one, who owed his lord <hi type="italic">a hundred measures of oil</hi> (in that commodity he paid his rent): <hi type="italic">Take thy bill,</hi> said he, here it is, and <hi type="italic">sit down quickly, and write fifty</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.6">v. 6</reference>); so he reduced his debt to the one half. Observe, he was in haste to have it done: "<hi type="italic">Sit down quickly,</hi> and do it, lest we be taken treating, and suspected." He took another, who owed his lord <hi type="italic">a hundred measures of wheat,</hi> and from his bill he cut off a fifth part, and bade him write <hi type="italic">fourscore</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.7">v. 7</reference>); probably he did the like by others, abating more or less according as he expected kindness from them. See here what uncertain things our worldly possessions are; they are most so to those who have most of them, who devolve upon others all the care concerning them, and so put it into their power to <hi type="italic">cheat them,</hi> because they will not trouble themselves to see with their own eyes. See also what treachery is to be found even among those in whom trust is reposed. How hard is it to find one that confidence can be reposed in! <hi type="italic">Let God be true, but every man a liar.</hi> Though this steward is turned out for dealing dishonestly, yet still he does so. So rare is it for men to mend of a fault, though they smart for it. <div eID="gen26117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26118" type="x-p"/> 4. The approbation of this: <hi type="italic">The lord commended the unjust steward, because he had done wisely,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.16.8">v. 8</reference>. It may be meant of <hi type="italic">his lord,</hi> the lord of that servant, who, though he could not but be angry at his knavery, yet was pleased with his ingenuity and policy for himself; but, taking it so, the latter part of the verse must be the words of <hi type="italic">our Lord,</hi> and therefore I think the whole is meant of him. Christ did, as it were, say, "Now commend me to such a man as this, that knows how to do well for himself, how to improve a present opportunity, and how to provide for a future necessity." He does not commend him because he had done <hi type="italic">falsely</hi> to his master, but because he had done <hi type="italic">wisely</hi> for himself. Yet perhaps herein he did well for his master too, and but justly with the tenants. He knew what <hi type="italic">hard bargains</hi> he had <hi type="italic">set them,</hi> so that they could not <hi type="italic">pay their rent,</hi> but, having been screwed up by his rigour, were thrown <hi type="italic">behindhand,</hi> and they and their families were likely to go to ruin; in consideration of this, he now, at going off, did as he ought to do both in justice and charity, not only easing them of part of their arrears, but abating their rent for the future. <hi type="italic">How much owest thou?</hi> may mean, "What rent dost thou sit upon? Come, I will set thee an easier bargain, and yet no easier than what thou oughtest to have." He had been <hi type="italic">all for his lord,</hi> but now he begins to consider the tenants, that he might have <hi type="italic">their favour</hi> when he had lost <hi type="italic">his lord's.</hi> The abating of their rent would be a lasting kindness, and more likely to engage them than abating their arrears only. Now this forecast of his, for a comfortable subsistence in this world, shames our improvidence for another world: <hi type="italic">The children of this world,</hi> who choose and have their portions in it, <hi type="italic">are wiser for their generation,</hi> act more considerately, and better consult their worldly interest and advantage, than the <hi type="italic">children of light,</hi> who enjoy the gospel, in <hi type="italic">their generation,</hi> that is, in the concerns of their souls and eternity. Note, (1.) The wisdom of worldly people in the concerns of this world is to be <hi type="italic">imitated</hi> by us in the concerns of our souls: it is their principle to improve their opportunities, to do that first which is most needful, in summer and harvest to lay up for winter, to take a good bargain when it is offered them, to trust the <hi type="italic">faithful</hi> and not the <hi type="italic">false.</hi> O that we were thus wise in our spiritual affairs! (2.) The children of light are commonly <hi type="italic">outdone</hi> by the children of this world. Not that the children of this world are <hi type="italic">truly wise;</hi> it is only <hi type="italic">in their generation.</hi> But in that they are <hi type="italic">wiser than the children of light in theirs;</hi> for, though we are told that we must shortly be <hi type="italic">turned out of our stewardship,</hi> yet we do not provide as we were to be <hi type="italic">here always</hi> and as if there were not <hi type="italic">another life after this,</hi> and are not so solicitous as this steward was to provide for <hi type="italic">hereafter.</hi> Though as <hi type="italic">children of the light,</hi> that light to which life and immortality are brought by the gospel, we cannot but see <hi type="italic">another world</hi> before us, yet we do not prepare for it, do not send our best effects and best affections thither, as we should. <div eID="gen26118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26119" type="x-p"/> II. The application of this parable, and the inferences drawn from it (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.9">v. 9</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I say unto you,</hi> you my disciples" (for to them this parable is directed, <reference osisRef="Luke.16.1">v. 1</reference>), "though you have but little in this world, consider how you may do good with that little." Observe, <div eID="gen26119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26120" type="x-p"/> 1. What it is that our Lord Jesus here exhorts us to; to provide for our comfortable reception to the happiness of another world, by making good use of our possessions and enjoyments in this world: "<hi type="italic">Make to yourselves friends of the mammon of unrighteousness,</hi> as the steward with his lord's goods made his lord's tenants his friends." It is the wisdom of the men of this world so to manage their money as that they may have the benefit of it hereafter, and not for the present only; therefore they put it out to interest, buy land with it, put it into this or the other fund. Now we should learn of them to make use of our money so as that we may be the better for it hereafter in another world, as they do in hopes to be the better for it hereafter in this world; so <hi type="italic">cast it upon the waters</hi> as that we may <hi type="italic">find it again after many days,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.1">Eccl. xi. 1</reference>. And in our case, though whatever we have <hi type="italic">are our Lord's goods,</hi> yet, as long as we dispose of them among <hi type="italic">our Lord's tenants</hi> and for their advantage, it is so far from being reckoned a wrong to our Lord, that it is a duty to him as well as policy for ourselves. Note, (1.) The things of this world are the <hi type="italic">mammon of unrighteousness,</hi> or the false <hi type="italic">mammon,</hi> not only because often got by fraud and unrighteousness, but because those who trust to it for satisfaction and happiness will certainly be deceived; for riches are perishing things, and will disappoint those that raise their expectations from them. (2.) Though this <hi type="italic">mammon of unrighteousness</hi> is not to be <hi type="italic">trusted to</hi> for a happiness, yet it may and must be <hi type="italic">made use of</hi> in subserviency to our pursuit of that which is our happiness. Though we cannot find true satisfaction in it, yet we may <hi type="italic">make to ourselves friends</hi> with it, not by way of <hi type="italic">purchase or merit,</hi> but <hi type="italic">recommendation;</hi> so we may make God and Christ our friends, the good angels and saints our friends, and the poor our friends; and it is a desirable thing to be <hi type="italic">befriended</hi> in the account and state to come. (3.) At death we must all <hi type="italic">fail,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">hotan eklipete</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">when ye suffer an eclipse.</hi> Death eclipses us. A tradesman is said to <hi type="italic">fail</hi> when he becomes a <hi type="italic">bankrupt.</hi> We must all thus fail shortly; death shuts up the shop, seals up the hand. Our comforts and enjoyments on earth will <hi type="italic">all fail</hi> us; flesh and heart fail. (4.) It ought to be our great concern to make it sure to ourselves, that <hi type="italic">when</hi> we <hi type="italic">fail</hi> at death we may be <hi type="italic">received into everlasting habitations</hi> in heaven. The <hi type="italic">habitations</hi> in heaven are <hi type="italic">everlasting,</hi> not <hi type="italic">made with hands,</hi> but <hi type="italic">eternal,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.1">2 Cor. v. 1</reference>. Christ is gone before, to prepare a place for those that are his, and is there ready to <hi type="italic">receive them;</hi> the bosom of Abraham is ready to receive them, and, when a <hi type="italic">guard of angels</hi> carries them thither, a <hi type="italic">choir of angels</hi> is ready to receive them there. The poor saints that are gone before to glory will receive those that in this world distributed to their necessities. (5.) This is a good reason why we should use what we have in the world for the honour of God and the good of our brethren, that thus we may with them <hi type="italic">lay up in store a good bond,</hi> a good security, a good foundation <hi type="italic">for the time to come,</hi> for an eternity to come. See <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.17-1Tim.6.19">1 Tim. vi. 17-19</reference>, which explains this here. <div eID="gen26120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26121" type="x-p"/> 2. With what arguments he presses this exhortation to abound in works of piety and charity. <div eID="gen26121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26122" type="x-p"/> (1.) If we do not make a right use of the <hi type="italic">gifts of God's providence,</hi> how can we expect from him those present and future comforts which are the <hi type="italic">gifts of his spiritual grace?</hi> Our Saviour here compares these, and shows that though our faithful use of the things of this world cannot be thought to merit any favour at the hand of God, yet our unfaithfulness in the use of them may be justly reckoned a <hi type="italic">forfeiture</hi> of that grace which is necessary to bring us to glory, and that is it which our Saviour here shows, <reference osisRef="Luke.16.10-Luke.16.14">v. 10-14</reference>. <div eID="gen26122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26123" type="x-p"/> [1.] The riches of this world are the <hi type="italic">less;</hi> grace and glory are the <hi type="italic">greater.</hi> Now if we be unfaithful in the less, if we use the things of this world to other purposes than those for which they were given us, it may justly be feared that we should be so in the gifts of God's grace, that we should receive them also in vain, and therefore they will be denied us: <hi type="italic">He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much.</hi> He that serves God, and does good, with his money, will serve God, and do good, with the more noble and valuable talents of wisdom and grace, and spiritual gifts, and the earnests of heaven; but he that buries the <hi type="italic">one talent</hi> of this world's wealth will never improve the <hi type="italic">five talents</hi> of spiritual riches. God withholds his grace from covetous worldly people more than we are aware of. [2.] The riches of this world are <hi type="italic">deceitful</hi> and <hi type="italic">uncertain;</hi> they are the <hi type="italic">unrighteous mammon,</hi> which is hastening from us apace, and, if we would make any advantage of it, we must bestir ourselves quickly; if we do not, how can we expect to be entrusted with spiritual riches, which are the only <hi type="italic">true riches?</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.16.11">v. 11</reference>. Let us be convinced of this, that those are <hi type="italic">truly</hi> rich, and <hi type="italic">very</hi> rich, who are rich in <hi type="italic">faith,</hi> and rich <hi type="italic">towards God,</hi> rich in Christ, in the promises, and in the earnests of heaven; and therefore let us lay up our treasure in them, expect our portion from them, and mind them in the first place, the <hi type="italic">kingdom of God and the righteousness thereof,</hi> and then, if other things be added to us, use them <hi type="italic">in ordine ad spiritualia—with a spiritual reference,</hi> so that by using them well we may take the faster hold of the <hi type="italic">true riches,</hi> and may be qualified to receive yet <hi type="italic">more grace</hi> from God; <hi type="italic">for God giveth to a man that is good in his sight,</hi> that is, to a free-hearted charitable man, <hi type="italic">wisdom, and knowledge, and joy</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.26">Eccl. ii. 26</reference>); that is, to a man that is <hi type="italic">faithful in the unrighteous mammon,</hi> he gives the <hi type="italic">true riches.</hi> [3.] The riches of this world are <hi type="italic">another man's.</hi> They are <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ta allotria</hi></hi>, not <hi type="italic">our own;</hi> for they are foreign to the soul and its nature and interest. They are not <hi type="italic">our own;</hi> for they are God's; his title to them is prior and superior to ours; the property remains in him, we are but usufructuaries. They are <hi type="italic">another man's;</hi> we have them from others; we use them for others, and <hi type="italic">what good has the owner</hi> from his <hi type="italic">goods</hi> that <hi type="italic">increase,</hi> save <hi type="italic">the beholding of them with his eyes,</hi> while still <hi type="italic">they are increased that eat them;</hi> and we must shortly leave them to others, and we know not to whom? But spiritual and eternal riches are <hi type="italic">our own</hi> (they enter into the soul that becomes <hi type="italic">possessed</hi> of them) and <hi type="italic">inseparably;</hi> they are a good part that will never be taken away from us. If we make Christ our own, and the promises our own, and heaven our own, we have that which we may truly call <hi type="italic">our own.</hi> But how can we expect God should <hi type="italic">enrich us</hi> with these if we do not serve him with our worldly possessions, of which we are but stewards? <div eID="gen26123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26124" type="x-p"/> (2.) We have no other way to prove ourselves the servants of God than by giving up ourselves so entirely to his service as to make <hi type="italic">mammon,</hi> that is, all our worldly gain, serviceable to us in his service (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">No servant can serve two masters,</hi> whose commands are so inconsistent as those of God and <hi type="italic">mammon</hi> are. If a man will <hi type="italic">love</hi> the world, and <hi type="italic">hold to that,</hi> it cannot be but he will <hi type="italic">hate God</hi> and <hi type="italic">despise</hi> him. He will make all his pretensions of religion truckle to his secular interests and designs, and the things of God shall be made to help him in serving and seeking the world. But, on the other hand, if a man will <hi type="italic">love God,</hi> and <hi type="italic">adhere</hi> to him, he will comparatively <hi type="italic">hate</hi> the world (whenever God and the world come in competition) and will <hi type="italic">despise</hi> it, and make all his business and success in the world some way or other conducive to his furtherance in the business of religion; and the things of the world shall be made to help him in serving God and working out his salvation. The matter is here laid plainly before us: <hi type="italic">Ye cannot serve God and mammon.</hi> So divided are their interests that their services can never be <hi type="italic">compounded.</hi> If therefore we be determined to <hi type="italic">serve God,</hi> we must disclaim and abjure the service of the world. <div eID="gen26124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26125" type="x-p"/> 3. We are here told what entertainment this doctrine of Christ met with among the Pharisees, and what rebuke he gave them. <div eID="gen26125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26126" type="x-p"/> (1.) They wickedly <hi type="italic">ridiculed</hi> him, <reference osisRef="Luke.16.14">v. 14</reference>. <hi type="italic">The Pharisees, who were covetous, heard all these things,</hi> and could not contradict him, but <hi type="italic">they derided him.</hi> Let us consider this, [1.] As their <hi type="italic">sin,</hi> and the fruit of their <hi type="italic">covetousness,</hi> which was their reigning sin, their own iniquity. Note, Many that make a great profession of religion, have much knowledge, and abound in the exercise of devotion, are yet ruined by the love of the world; nor does any thing harden the heart more against the word of Christ. These covetous Pharisees could not bear to have that <hi type="italic">touched,</hi> which was their <hi type="italic">Delilah,</hi> their darling lust; for this they derided him, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">exemykterizon auton</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">they snuffled up their noses at him,</hi> or blew their noses on him. It is an expression of the utmost scorn and disdain imaginable; <hi type="italic">the word of the Lord was to them a reproach,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.6.10">Jer. vi. 10</reference>. They laughed at him for going so contrary to the opinion and way of the world, for endeavouring to recover them from a sin which they were resolved to hold fast. Note, It is common for those to <hi type="italic">make a jest</hi> of the word of God who are resolved that they will not be ruled by it; but they will find at last that it cannot be turned off so. [2.] As <hi type="italic">his suffering.</hi> Our Lord Jesus endured not only the <hi type="italic">contradiction</hi> of sinners, but their <hi type="italic">contempt;</hi> they <hi type="italic">had him in derision</hi> all the day. He that spoke as never man spoke was bantered and ridiculed, that his faithful ministers, whose preaching is unjustly <hi type="italic">derided,</hi> may not be disheartened at it. It is no disgrace to a man to be laughed at, but to deserve to be laughed at. Christ's apostles were <hi type="italic">mocked,</hi> and no wonder; the <hi type="italic">disciple is not greater than his Lord.</hi> <div eID="gen26126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26127" type="x-p"/> (2.) He justly reproved them; not for <hi type="italic">deriding</hi> him (he knew how to <hi type="italic">despise the shame</hi>), but for <hi type="italic">deceiving</hi> themselves with the shows and colours of piety, when they were strangers to the power of it, <reference osisRef="Luke.16.15">v. 15</reference>. Here is, <div eID="gen26127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26128" type="x-p"/> [1.] Their <hi type="italic">specious outside;</hi> nay, it was a <hi type="italic">splendid one. First,</hi> They <hi type="italic">justified themselves before men;</hi> they denied whatever ill was laid to their charge, even by Christ himself. They claimed to be looked upon as men of singular sanctity and devotion, and justified themselves in that claim: "<hi type="italic">You are they that</hi> do that, so as none ever did, that make it your business to court the opinion of men, and, right or wrong, will justify yourselves before the world; you are <hi type="italic">notorious</hi> for this." <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> They were <hi type="italic">highly esteemed among men.</hi> Men did not only <hi type="italic">acquit</hi> them from any blame they were under, but <hi type="italic">applauded</hi> them, and had them in veneration, not only as <hi type="italic">good men,</hi> but as the <hi type="italic">best of men.</hi> Their sentiments were esteemed as oracles, their directions as laws, and their practices as inviolable prescriptions. <div eID="gen26128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26129" type="x-p"/> [2.] Their <hi type="italic">odious inside,</hi> which was under the eye of God: "He <hi type="italic">knows your heart,</hi> and it is in his sight an <hi type="italic">abomination;</hi> for it is full of all manner of wickedness." Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It is folly to <hi type="italic">justify ourselves before men,</hi> and to think this enough to bear us out, and bring us off, in the judgment of the great day, that men <hi type="italic">know no ill</hi> of us; for God, who knows our hearts, knows that ill of us which no one else can know. This ought to check our value for ourselves, and our confidence in ourselves, that <hi type="italic">God knows our hearts,</hi> and how much deceit is there, for we have reason to abase and distrust ourselves. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It is folly to judge of persons and things by the opinion of men concerning them, and to go down with the stream of vulgar estimate; for that which is <hi type="italic">highly esteemed among men,</hi> who judge according to outward appearance, is perhaps <hi type="italic">an abomination in the sight of God,</hi> who sees things as they are, and whose judgment, we are sure, is according to truth. On the contrary, there are those whom men despise and condemn who yet are accepted and approved of God, <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.18">2 Cor. x. 18</reference>. <div eID="gen26129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26130" type="x-p"/> (3.) He turned from them to the publicans and sinners, as more likely to be wrought upon by his gospel than those covetous conceited Pharisees (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.16">v. 16</reference>): "The <hi type="italic">law and the prophets were</hi> indeed <hi type="italic">until John;</hi> the Old-Testament dispensation, which was <hi type="italic">confined</hi> to you Jews, continued till John Baptist appeared, and you seemed to have the monopoly of righteousness and salvation; and you are puffed up with this, and this gains you esteem among men, that you are students in the law and the prophets; but since John Baptist appeared <hi type="italic">the kingdom of God is preached,</hi> a New-Testament dispensation, which does not value men at all for their being doctors of the law, but <hi type="italic">every man presses</hi> into the gospel kingdom, Gentiles as well as Jews, and no man thinks himself bound in good manners to let his betters go before him into it, or to stay till the <hi type="italic">rulers</hi> and the Pharisees have led him that way. It is not so much a political national constitution as the Jewish economy was, when <hi type="italic">salvation was of the Jews;</hi> but it is made a particular personal concern, and therefore <hi type="italic">every man</hi> that is convinced he has a soul to save, and an eternity to provide for, thrusts to get in, lest he should come short by trifling and complimenting." Some give this sense of it; they derided Christ or speaking in contempt of riches, for, thought they, were there not many promises of riches and other temporal good things in the <hi type="italic">law and the prophets?</hi> And were not many of the best of God's servants very rich, as Abraham and David? "It is true," saith Christ, "so it was, but now that the kingdom of God is begun to be preached things take a new turn; now blessed are the poor, and the mourners, and the persecuted." The Pharisees, to requite the people for their high opinion of them, allowed them in a cheap, easy, formal religion. "But," saith Christ, "now that the <hi type="italic">gospel is preached</hi> the eyes of the people are opened, and as they cannot now have a veneration for the Pharisees, as they have had, so they cannot content themselves with such an indifferency in religion as they have been trained up in, but they <hi type="italic">press</hi> with a holy violence into the kingdom of God." Note, Those that would go to heaven must take pains, must strive against the stream, must press against the crowd that are going the contrary way. <div eID="gen26130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26131" type="x-p"/> (4.) Yet still he protests against any design to invalidate the law (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">It is easier for heaven and earth to pass,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">parelthein</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">to pass by,</hi> to pass away, though the foundations of the earth and the pillars of heaven are so firmly established, <hi type="italic">than for one tittle of the law to fail.</hi> The moral law is confirmed and ratified, and not one tittle of that fails; the duties enjoined by it are duties still; the sins forbidden by it are sins still. Nay, the precepts of it are explained and enforced by the gospel, and made to appear more spiritual. The ceremonial law is perfected in the gospel colours; not <hi type="italic">one tittle</hi> of that <hi type="italic">fails,</hi> for it is found printed off in the gospel, where, though the force of it is as a law taken off, yet the figure of it as a type shines very brightly, witness the epistle to the Hebrews. There were some things which were connived at by the law, for the preventing of greater mischiefs, the permission of which the gospel has indeed taken away, but without any detriment or disparagement to the law, for it has thereby reduced them to the primitive intention of the law, as in the case of divorce (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.18">v. 18</reference>), which we had before, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.32">Matt. v. 32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.19.9">xix. 9</reference>. Christ will not allow divorces, for his gospel is intended to strike at the bitter root of men's corrupt appetites and passions, to kill them, and pluck them up; and therefore they must not be so far <hi type="italic">indulged</hi> as that permission <hi type="italic">did</hi> indulge them, for the more they are indulged the more impetuous and headstrong they grow.
entries.668d4b70ca18978575455eddcc7413c3d449469f: <div eID="gen26131" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Rich Man and Lazarus.</title> <div sID="gen26132" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> There was a certain rich man, which was clothed in purple and fine linen, and fared sumptuously every day: 20 And there was a certain beggar named Lazarus, which was laid at his gate, full of sores, <hi type="super">21</hi> And desiring to be fed with the crumbs which fell from the rich man's table: moreover the dogs came and licked his sores. <hi type="super">22</hi> And it came to pass, that the beggar died, and was carried by the angels into Abraham's bosom: the rich man also died, and was buried; <hi type="super">23</hi> And in hell he lift up his eyes, being in torments, and seeth Abraham afar off, and Lazarus in his bosom. <hi type="super">24</hi> And he cried and said, Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water, and cool my tongue; for I am tormented in this flame. <hi type="super">25</hi> But Abraham said, Son, remember that thou in thy lifetime receivedst thy good things, and likewise Lazarus evil things: but now he is comforted, and thou art tormented. <hi type="super">26</hi> And beside all this, between us and you there is a great gulf fixed: so that they which would pass from hence to you cannot; neither can they pass to us, that <hi type="italic">would come</hi> from thence. <hi type="super">27</hi> Then he said, I pray thee therefore, father, that thou wouldest send him to my father's house: <hi type="super">28</hi> For I have five brethren; that he may testify unto them, lest they also come into this place of torment. <hi type="super">29</hi> Abraham saith unto him, They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them. <hi type="super">30</hi> And he said, Nay, father Abraham: but if one went unto them from the dead, they will repent. <hi type="super">31</hi> And he said unto him, If they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead. <div eID="gen26132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26133" type="x-p"/> As the parable of the prodigal son set before us the grace of the gospel, which is encouraging to us all, so this sets before us the <hi type="italic">wrath to come,</hi> and is designed for our awakening; and very fast asleep those are in sin that will not be awakened by it. The Pharisees made a jest of Christ's sermon against worldliness; now this parable was intended to make those mockers serious. The tendency of the gospel of Christ is both to reconcile us to poverty and affliction and to arm us against temptations to worldliness and sensuality. Now this parable, by drawing the curtain, and letting us see what will be the end of both in the other world, goes very far in prosecuting those two great intentions. This parable is not like Christ's other parables, in which spiritual things are represented by similitudes borrowed from worldly things, as those of the sower and the seed (except that of the sheep and goats), the prodigal son, and indeed all the rest but this. But here the <hi type="italic">spiritual things themselves</hi> are represented in a narrative or description of the different state of good and bad in this world and the other. Yet we need not call it a history of a particular occurrence, but it is <hi type="italic">matter of fact</hi> that is true every day, that poor godly people, whom men neglect and trample upon, die away out of their miseries, and go to heavenly bliss and joy, which is made the more pleasant to them by their preceding sorrows; and that rich epicures, who live in luxury, and are unmerciful to the poor, die, and go into a state of insupportable torment, which is the more grievous and terrible to them because of the sensual lives they lived: and that there is no gaining any relief from their torments. Is this a parable? What similitude is there in this? The discourse indeed between Abraham and the rich man is only an illustration of the description, to make it the more affecting, like that between God and Satan in the story of Job. Our Saviour came to bring us acquainted with another world, and to show us the reference which <hi type="italic">this</hi> world has to <hi type="italic">that;</hi> and here is does it. In this description (for so I shall choose to call it) we may observe, <div eID="gen26133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26134" type="x-p"/> I. The different condition of a <hi type="italic">wicked rich man,</hi> and a <hi type="italic">godly poor man,</hi> in this world. We know that as some of late, so the Jews of old, were ready to make prosperity one of the marks of a true church, of a good man and a favourite of heaven, so that they could hardly have any favourable thoughts of a <hi type="italic">poor man.</hi> This mistake Christ, upon all occasions, set himself to correct, and here very fully, where we have, <div eID="gen26134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26135" type="x-p"/> 1. A wicked man, and one that will be for ever miserable, in the height of prosperity (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.19">v. 19</reference>): <hi type="italic">There was a certain rich man.</hi> From the Latin we commonly call him <hi type="italic">Dives—a rich man;</hi> but, as Bishop Tillotson observes, he has no name given him, as the poor man has, because it had been invidious to have named any particular rich man in such a description as this, and apt to provoke and gain ill-will. But others observe that Christ would not do the rich man so much honour as to name him, though when perhaps he called his lands by his own name he thought it should long survive that of the beggar at his gate, which yet is here preserved, when that of the rich man is buried in oblivion. Now we are told concerning this rich man, <div eID="gen26135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26136" type="x-p"/> (1.) That he was <hi type="italic">clothed in purple and fine linen,</hi> and that was his <hi type="italic">adorning.</hi> He had <hi type="italic">fine linen</hi> for <hi type="italic">pleasure,</hi> and clean, no doubt, every day; night-linen, and day-linen. He had <hi type="italic">purple</hi> for <hi type="italic">state,</hi> for that was the wear of princes, which has made some conjecture that Christ had an eye to Herod in it. He never appeared abroad but in great magnificence. <div eID="gen26136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26137" type="x-p"/> (2.) He <hi type="italic">fared</hi> deliciously and <hi type="italic">sumptuously every day.</hi> His table was furnished with all the varieties and dainties that nature and art could supply; his side-table richly adorned with plate; his servants, who waited at table, in rich liveries; and the guests at his table, no doubt, such as he thought <hi type="italic">graced</hi> it. Well, and what harm was there in all this? It is no sin to be rich, no sin to wear purple and fine linen, nor to keep a plentiful table, if a man's estate will afford it. Not are we told that he got his estate by fraud, oppression, or extortion, no, nor that he was drunk, or made others drunk; but, [1.] Christ would hereby show that a man may have a great deal of the wealth, and pomp, and pleasure of this world, and yet lie and perish for ever under God's wrath and curse. We cannot infer from men's living great either that God loves them <hi type="italic">in</hi> giving them so much, or that they love God <hi type="italic">for</hi> giving them so much; happiness consists not in these things. [2.] That plenty and pleasure are a very <hi type="italic">dangerous</hi> and to many a <hi type="italic">fatal</hi> temptation to luxury, and sensuality, and forgetfulness of God and another world. This man might have been happy if he had not had great possessions and enjoyments. [3.] That the indulgence of the body, and the ease and pleasure of that, are the ruin of many a soul, and the interests of it. It is true, eating good meat and wearing good clothes are lawful; but it is true that they often become the food and fuel of pride and luxury, and so turn into sin to us. [4.] That feasting ourselves and our friends, and, at the same time, forgetting the distresses of the poor and afflicted, are very provoking to God and damning to the soul. The sin of this rich man was not so much his dress or his diet, but his providing only for himself. <div eID="gen26137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26138" type="x-p"/> 2. Here is a godly man, and one that will be for ever happy, in the depth of adversity and distress (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">There was a certain beggar,</hi> named <hi type="italic">Lazarus.</hi> A beggar of that name, eminently devout, and in great distress, was probably well known among good people at that time: a beggar, suppose such a one as Eleazar, or Lazarus. Some think Eleazar a proper name for any poor man, for it signifies the <hi type="italic">help of God,</hi> which they must fly to that are destitute of <hi type="italic">other helps.</hi> This poor man was reduced to the last extremity, as miserable, as to outward things, as you can lightly suppose a man to be in this world. <div eID="gen26138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26139" type="x-p"/> (1.) His body was <hi type="italic">full of sores,</hi> like Job. To be sick and weak in body is a great affliction; but sores are more <hi type="italic">painful</hi> to the patient, and more <hi type="italic">loathsome</hi> to those about him. <div eID="gen26139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26140" type="x-p"/> (2.) He was forced to beg his bread, and to take up with such scraps as he could get at rich people's doors. He was so sore and lame that he could not go himself, but was carried by some compassionate hand or other, and <hi type="italic">laid at the rich man's gate.</hi> Note, Those that are not able to help the poor with their <hi type="italic">purses</hi> should help them with their <hi type="italic">pains;</hi> those that cannot lend them <hi type="italic">a penny</hi> should lend them <hi type="italic">a hand;</hi> those that have not themselves wherewithal to give to them should either bring them, or go for them, to those that have. Lazarus, in his distress, had nothing of his own to subsist on, no relation to go to, nor did the parish take care of him. It is an instance of the degeneracy of the Jewish church at this time that such a godly man as Lazarus was should be suffered to perish for want of necessary food. Now observe, <div eID="gen26140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26141" type="x-p"/> [1.] His expectations from the rich man's table: <hi type="italic">He desired to be fed with the crumbs,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.16.21">v. 21</reference>. He did not look for a mess from off his table, though he ought to have had one, one of the best; but would be thankful for the crumbs from under the table, the broken meat which was the rich man's leavings; nay, the leavings of his dogs. <hi type="italic">The poor use entreaties,</hi> and must be content with such as they can get. Now this is taken notice of to show, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> What was the distress, and what the disposition, of the poor man. He was <hi type="italic">poor,</hi> but he was <hi type="italic">poor in spirit,</hi> contentedly poor. He did not lie at the rich man's gate complaining, and bawling, and making a noise, but silently and modestly desiring to be <hi type="italic">fed with the crumbs.</hi> This miserable man was a good man, and in favour with God. Note, It is often the lot of some of the dearest of God's saints and servants to be greatly afflicted in this world, while wicked people prosper, and have abundance; see <reference osisRef="Ps.73.7">Ps. lxxiii. 7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.73.10">10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.73.14">14</reference>. Here is a child of wrath and an heir of hell sitting in the house, faring sumptuously; and a child of love and an heir of heaven lying at the gate, perishing for hunger. And is men's spiritual state to be judged of then by their outward condition? <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> What was the temper of the rich man towards him. We are not told that he abused him, or forbade him his gate, or did him any harm, but it is intimated that he slighted him; he had no concern for him, took no care about him. Here was a <hi type="italic">real</hi> object of charity, and a very <hi type="italic">moving</hi> one, which spoke for itself; it was presented to him at <hi type="italic">his own gate.</hi> The poor man had a good character and good conduct, and every thing that could recommend him. A <hi type="italic">little</hi> thing would be a <hi type="italic">great</hi> kindness to him, and yet he took no cognizance of his case, did not order him to be taken in and lodged in the barn, or some of the out-buildings, but let him lie there. Note, It is not enough not to oppress and trample upon the poor; we shall be found unfaithful stewards of our Lord's goods, in the great day, if we do not succour and relieve them. The reason given for the most fearful doom is, <hi type="italic">I was hungry, and you gave me no meat.</hi> I wonder how those rich people who have read the gospel of Christ, and way that they believe it, can be so unconcerned as they often are in the necessities and miseries of the poor and afflicted. <div eID="gen26141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26142" type="x-p"/> [2.] The usage he had from the dogs; <hi type="italic">The dogs came and licked his sores.</hi> The rich man kept a kennel of hounds, it may be, or other dogs, for his diversion, and to please his fancy, and these were fed to the full, when poor Lazarus could not get enough to keep him alive. Note, Those will have a great deal to answer for hereafter that feed their dogs, but neglect the poor. And it is a great aggravation of the uncharitableness of many rich people that they bestow that upon their fancies and follies which would supply the necessity, and rejoice the heart, of many a good Christian in distress. Those offend God, nay, and they put a contempt upon human nature, that pamper their dogs and horses, and let the families of their poor neighbours starve. Now those dogs <hi type="italic">came and licked the</hi> sores of poor Lazarus, which may be taken, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> As an aggravation of his misery. His sores were <hi type="italic">bloody,</hi> which tempted the dogs to come, and lick them, as they did the blood of Naboth and Ahab, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.21.19">1 Kings xxi. 19</reference>. And we read of the <hi type="italic">tongue of the dogs dipped</hi> in the <hi type="italic">blood of enemies,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.68.23">Ps. lxviii. 23</reference>. They attacked him while he was yet alive, as if he had been already dead, and he had not strength himself to keep them off, nor would any of the servants be so civil as to check them. The dogs were like their master, and thought they fared sumptuously when they regaled themselves with human gore. Or, it may be taken, <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> as some relief to him in his misery; <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">alla kai</hi></hi>, the master was <hi type="italic">hard-hearted</hi> towards him, <hi type="italic">but</hi> the dogs <hi type="italic">came and licked his sores,</hi> which mollified and eased them. It is not said, They <hi type="italic">sucked</hi> them, but <hi type="italic">licked</hi> them, which was good for them. The dogs were more kind to him than their master was. <div eID="gen26142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26143" type="x-p"/> II. Here is the <hi type="italic">different condition</hi> of this <hi type="italic">godly poor man,</hi> and this <hi type="italic">wicked rich man, at</hi> and <hi type="italic">after death.</hi> Hitherto the wicked man seems to have the advantage, but <hi type="italic">Exitus acta probat</hi>—<hi type="italic">Let us wait awhile, to see the end hereof.</hi> <div eID="gen26143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26144" type="x-p"/> 1. They both died (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.22">v. 22</reference>): The <hi type="italic">beggar died;</hi> the <hi type="italic">rich man also died.</hi> Death is the common lot of rich and poor, godly and ungodly; there they meet together. One dieth <hi type="italic">in his full strength,</hi> and another in <hi type="italic">the bitterness of his soul;</hi> but they shall <hi type="italic">lie down alike in the dust,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.21.26">Job xxi. 26</reference>. Death favours not either the rich man for his riches or the poor man for his poverty. Saints die, that they may bring their sorrows to an end, and may enter upon their joys. Sinners die, that they may go to give up their account. It concerns both rich and poor to prepare for death, for it waits for them both. <hi type="italic">Mors sceptra ligonibus æquat—Death blends the sceptre with the spade.</hi> <div eID="gen26144" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen26145"/> <l level="1" sID="gen26146"/>———æquo pulsat pede pauperum tabernas,<l eID="gen26146" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen26147"/>Regumque turres.<l eID="gen26147" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen26148"/>With equal pace, impartial fate<l eID="gen26148" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen26149"/>Knocks at the palace, as the cottage gate.<l eID="gen26149" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen26145"/> <div sID="gen26150" type="x-p"/> 2. The beggar <hi type="italic">died first.</hi> God often takes godly people out of the world, when he leaves the wicked to flourish still. It was an advantage to the beggar that such a speedy end was put to his miseries; and, since he could find no other shelter or resting-place, he was <hi type="italic">hid in the grave,</hi> where the <hi type="italic">weary are at rest.</hi> <div eID="gen26150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26151" type="x-p"/> 3. The rich man <hi type="italic">died and was buried.</hi> Nothing is said of the interment of the poor man. They dug a hole any where, and tumbled his body in, without any solemnity; he was <hi type="italic">buried with the burial of an ass:</hi> nay, it is well if they that let the dogs lick his sores did not let them gnaw his bones. The beggar died and was <hi type="italic">carried by angels into Abraham's bosom.</hi> How much did the honour done to his soul, by this convoy of it to its rest, exceed the honour done to the rich man, by the carrying of his body with so much magnificence to its grave! Here is an account of what passed between the rich man and Abraham in the separate state—a state of separation one from another, and of both from this world. Though it is probable that there will not be, nor are, any such dialogues or discourses between glorified saints and damned sinners, yet it is very proper, and what is usually done in descriptions, especially such as are designed to be pathetic and moving, by such dialogues to represent what will be the mind and sentiments both of the one and of the other. And since we find damned sinners tormented <hi type="italic">in the presence of the Lamb</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.14.10">Rev. xiv. 10</reference>), and the faithful servants of God looking upon them that have <hi type="italic">transgressed the covenant,</hi> there where their <hi type="italic">worm dies not, and their fire is not quenched</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.66.23-Isa.66.24">Isa. lxvi. 23, 24</reference>), such a discourse as this is not incongruous to be supposed. He that used to <hi type="italic">command</hi> aloud now <hi type="italic">begs</hi> aloud, louder than ever Lazarus did at his gate. The representation he makes to him of his present deplorable condition: <hi type="italic">I am tormented in this flame.</hi> It is the torment of his soul that he complains of, and therefore such a fire as will operate upon souls; and such a fire the <hi type="italic">wrath of God</hi> is, fastening upon a guilty conscience; such a fire horror of mind is, and the reproaches of a self-accusing self-condemning heart. His request to Abraham, in consideration of this misery: <hi type="italic">Have mercy on me.</hi> Note, The day is coming when those that make light of divine mercy will beg hard for it. He that had no mercy on Lazarus, yet expects Lazarus should have mercy on him; "for," thinks he, "Lazarus is better natured than ever I was." The further request he had to make to his father Abraham, not for himself, his mouth is stopped, and he has not a word to say in answer to Abraham's denial of a drop of water. When he was on earth he might have prayed and been heard, but now he prays in vain. "<hi type="italic">Therefore,</hi> because thou hast denied me the former request, surely thou wilt be so compassionate as not to deny this:" or, "<hi type="italic">Therefore,</hi> because <hi type="italic">there is a great gulf fixed,</hi> seeing there is no getting out hence when they are once here, O send to prevent their coming hither:" or, "Though there is a <hi type="italic">great gulf fixed</hi> between you and me, yet, since there is no such gulf fixed between you and them, send them hither. Send him back <hi type="italic">to my father's house;</hi> he knows well enough where it is, has been there many a time, having been denied the crumbs that fell from the table. He knows I have <hi type="italic">five brethren</hi> there; if he appear to them, they will <hi type="italic">know him,</hi> and will regard what he saith, for they knew him to be an honest man. Let him <hi type="italic">testify to them;</hi> let him tell them what condition I am in, and that I brought myself to it by my luxury and sensuality, and my unmercifulness to the poor. Let him warn them not to tread in my steps, nor to go on in the way wherein I led them, and left them, <hi type="italic">lest they also come into this place of torment,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Luke.16.28">v. 28</reference>. Some observe that he speaks only of <hi type="italic">five brethren,</hi> whence they infer that he had <hi type="italic">no children,</hi> else he would have mentioned them, and then it was an aggravation of his uncharitableness that he had no children to provide for. Now he would have them stopped in their sinful course. He does not say, "Give me leave to go to them, that I may testify to them;" for he knew that there was a <hi type="italic">gulf fixed,</hi> and despaired of a permission so favourable to himself: his going would frighten them out of their <hi type="italic">wits;</hi> but, "Send Lazarus, whose address will be less terrible, and yet his testimony sufficient to frighten them out of their <hi type="italic">sins.</hi>" Now he desired the preventing of their ruin, partly in tenderness to <hi type="italic">them,</hi> for whom he could not but retain a <hi type="italic">natural affection;</hi> he knew their temper, their temptations, their ignorance, their infidelity, their inconsideration, and wished to prevent the destruction they were running into: but it was partly in tenderness <hi type="italic">to himself,</hi> for their coming to him, to that <hi type="italic">place of torment,</hi> would but aggravate the misery to him, who had helped to show them the way thither, as the sight of Lazarus helped to aggravate his misery. When partners in sin come to be sharers in woe, as tares bound in bundles for the fire, they will be a terror to one another. <div eID="gen26167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26168" type="x-p"/> (2.) Abraham denies him this favour too. There is no request granted in hell. Those who make the rich man's praying to Abraham a justification of their praying to saints departed, as they have far to seek for proofs, when the practice of a damned sinner must be valued for an example, so they have little encouragement to follow the example, when all his prayers were made <hi type="italic">in vain.</hi> Abraham leaves them to the testimony of Moses and the prophets, the ordinary means of conviction and conversion; they have the written word, which they may read and hear read. "<hi type="italic">Let them</hi> attend to that <hi type="italic">sure word of prophecy,</hi> for God will not go out of the common method of his grace for them." Here is their privilege: <hi type="italic">They have Moses and the prophets;</hi> and their duty: "<hi type="italic">Let them hear them,</hi> and mix faith with them, and that will be sufficient to keep them from this place of torment." By this it appears that there is sufficient evidence in the Old Testament, in Moses and <hi type="italic">the prophets,</hi> to convince those that will hear them impartially that there is another life after this, and a state of rewards and punishments for good and bad men; for that was the thing which the rich man would have his brethren assured of, and for that they are turned over to Moses and the prophets. <div eID="gen26168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26169" type="x-p"/> (3.) He urges his request yet further (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.30">v. 30</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Nay, father Abraham,</hi> give me leave to press this. It is true, they have Moses and the prophets, and, if they would but give a due regard to them, it would be sufficient; but they do not, they will not; yet it may be hoped, <hi type="italic">if one went to them from the dead, they would repent,</hi> that would be a more sensible conviction to them. They are used to Moses and the prophets, and therefore regard them the less; but this would be a <hi type="italic">new thing,</hi> and more startling; surely this would bring them to <hi type="italic">repent,</hi> and to change their wicked habit and course of life." Note, Foolish men are apt to think any method of conviction better than that which God has chosen and appointed.  <chapter eID="Luke.16"/> <div eID="gen26169" type="x-p"/>

entries.82ec271c2a35babbbe28723c8edd8e2b0e8bd05a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14598"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 16</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Luke.16.1-Luke.16.31">Lu 16:1-31</reference>. Parables of the Unjust Steward and of the Rich Man and Lazarus, or, the Right Use of Money.</title> <div sID="gen28224" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14598"/><hi type="bold">1. steward--</hi>manager of his estate.<div eID="gen28224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28225" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">accused--</hi>informed upon.<div eID="gen28225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28226" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">had wasted--</hi>rather, "was wasting." <div eID="gen28226" type="x-p"/>
entries.82c6338854185eb61ff8c1175727fdfa2330c343: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14599"/><div sID="gen28227" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14599"/><hi type="bold">3. cannot dig ... to beg, ashamed--</hi>therefore, when dismissed, shall be in utter want. <div eID="gen28227" type="x-p"/>
entries.d1de6f371b27353e39b211218af6c597a9874303: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14600"/><div sID="gen28228" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14600"/><hi type="bold">4. may receive me, &c.--</hi>Observe his one object--when cast out of one home to secure another. This is the key to the parable, on which there have been many differing views. <div eID="gen28228" type="x-p"/>
entries.547cead92a887f6d538931d2b597f0f053437c0b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14601"/><div sID="gen28229" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14601"/><hi type="bold">5-7. fifty ... fourscore--</hi>deducting a half from the debt of the one, and a fifth from that of the other. <div eID="gen28229" type="x-p"/>
entries.6c0393af529f526f264660af5781ce6e872ced2e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14602"/><div sID="gen28230" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14602"/><hi type="bold">8. the lord--</hi>evidently the steward's lord, so called in <reference osisRef="Luke.16.3">Lu 16:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.16.5">5</reference>.<div eID="gen28230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28231" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">commended, &c.--</hi>not for his "injustice," but "because he had done wisely," or prudently; with commendable foresight and skilful adaptation of means to end.<div eID="gen28231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28232" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">children of this world--</hi>so <reference osisRef="Luke.20.34">Lu 20:34</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Ps.17.14">Psa 17:14</reference> ("their portion in this life"); <reference osisRef="Phil.3.19">Php 3:19</reference> ("mind earthly things"); <reference osisRef="Ps.4.6">Psa 4:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.4.7">7</reference>.<div eID="gen28232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28233" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their generation--</hi>or "for their generation"--that is, for the purposes of the "world" they are "of." The greater wisdom (or shrewdness) of the one, in adaptation of means to ends, and in energetic, determined prosecution of them, is none of it for God and eternity--a region they were never in, an atmosphere they never breathed, an undiscovered world, an unborn existence to them--but all for the purposes of their own grovelling and fleeting generation.<div eID="gen28233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28234" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">children of light--</hi>(so <reference osisRef="John.12.36">Joh 12:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.8">Ep 5:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.5">1Th 5:5</reference>). Yet this is only "as night-birds see better in the dark than those of the day owls than eagles" [Cajetan and Trench]. But we may learn lessons from them, as our Lord now shows, and "be wise as serpents." <div eID="gen28234" type="x-p"/>
entries.1ee4a65badef0de0be46eca434688087ebdf9fc5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14603"/><div sID="gen28235" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14603"/><hi type="bold">9. Make ... friends of--</hi>Turn to your advantage; that is, as the steward did, "by showing mercy to the poor" (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.27">Da 4:27</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Luke.12.33">Lu 12:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.14.13">14:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.14.14">14</reference>).<div eID="gen28235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28236" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mammon of unrighteousness--</hi>treacherous, precarious. (See on <reference osisRef="Matt.6.24">Mt 6:24</reference>).<div eID="gen28236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28237" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye fail--</hi>in respect of life.<div eID="gen28237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28238" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they may receive you--</hi>not generally, "ye may be received" (as <reference osisRef="Luke.6.38">Lu 6:38</reference>, "shall men give"), but "those ye have relieved may rise up as witnesses for you" at the great day. Then, like the steward, when turned out of one home shall ye secure another; but better than he, a heavenly for an earthly, an everlasting for a temporary habitation. Money is not here made the key to heaven, more than "the deeds done in the body" in general, according to which, as a test of character--but not by the merit of which--men are to be judged (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.10">2Co 5:10</reference>, and see <reference osisRef="Matt.25.34-Matt.25.40">Mt 25:34-40</reference>). <div eID="gen28238" type="x-p"/>
entries.7ee418fc0a7087cb4d1d6ecfdbc72fd676726d55: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14604"/><div sID="gen28239" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14604"/><hi type="bold">10. He, &c.--</hi>a maxim of great pregnancy and value; rising from the prudence which the steward had to the fidelity which he had not, the "harmlessness of the dove, to which the serpent" with all his "wisdom" is a total stranger. Fidelity depends not on the amount entrusted, but on the sense of responsibility. He that feels this in little will feel it in much, and conversely. <div eID="gen28239" type="x-p"/>
entries.2753608faaf7f5cf0ccb9b7ed7e6dfa62cf21f41: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14605"/><div sID="gen28240" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14605"/><hi type="bold">11-12. unrighteous mammon--</hi>To the whole of this He applies the disparaging term "what is least," in contrast with "the true riches." <div eID="gen28240" type="x-p"/>
entries.7dc1833203431352a3df8f4eb26f19dd8af78ee1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14607"/><div sID="gen28242" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14607"/><hi type="bold">13. can serve--</hi>be entirely at the command of; and this is true even where the services are not opposed.<div eID="gen28242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28243" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hate ... love--</hi>showing that the two here intended are in uncompromising hostility to each other: an awfully searching principle! <div eID="gen28243" type="x-p"/>
entries.758fe4a38f19d9f48f5cc1a1edb1870aa3da392a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14608"/><div sID="gen28244" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14608"/><hi type="bold">14-18. covetous ... derided him--</hi>sneered at Him; their master sin being too plainly struck at for them to relish. But it was easier to run down than to refute such teaching. <div eID="gen28244" type="x-p"/>
entries.570aae6b5822ebd36a23e443ea72329a58de05a0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14613"/><div sID="gen28251" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14613"/><hi type="bold">19. purple and fine linen, &c.--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Esth.8.15">Es 8:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.18.12">Re 18:12</reference>); wanting nothing which taste and appetite craved and money could procure. <div eID="gen28251" type="x-p"/>
entries.d8b2033bf4a1773a4b4c8efb329af10954e5ac84: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14614"/><div sID="gen28252" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14614"/><hi type="bold">20-21. laid--</hi>having to be carried and put down.<div eID="gen28252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28253" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">full of sores--</hi>open, running, "not closed, nor bound up, nor mollified with ointment" (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.6">Is 1:6</reference>). <div eID="gen28253" type="x-p"/>
entries.494b6199ed42a5bcce7240cb7242c97750c4f24a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14616"/><div sID="gen28256" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14616"/><hi type="bold">22. died--</hi>His burial was too unimportant to mention; while "the rich man died and was buried"--his carcass carried in pomp to its earthly resting-place.<div eID="gen28256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28257" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in to Abraham's bosom--</hi>as if seen reclining next to Him at the heavenly feast (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.11">Mt 8:11</reference>). <div eID="gen28257" type="x-p"/>
entries.07c48fd01f216b4714442a456bd710d6d08a1870: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14617"/><div sID="gen28258" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14617"/><hi type="bold">23. in hell--</hi>not the final place of the lost (for which another word is used), but as we say "the unseen world." But as the object here is certainly to depict the whole torment of the one and the perfect bliss of the other, it comes in this case to much the same.<div eID="gen28258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28259" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seeth Abraham--</hi>not God, to whom therefore he cannot cry [Bengel]. <div eID="gen28259" type="x-p"/>
entries.261f345348c3d8d26f1230fc3325b2170a13bd77: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14618"/><div sID="gen28260" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14618"/><hi type="bold">24. Father Abraham--</hi>a well-founded, but unavailing, claim of natural descent (<reference osisRef="Luke.3.8">Lu 3:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.8.37">Joh 8:37</reference>).<div eID="gen28260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28261" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">mercy on me--</hi>who never showed any (<reference osisRef="Jas.2.3">Jas 2:3</reference>).<div eID="gen28261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28262" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">send Lazarus--</hi>the pining victim of his merciless neglect.<div eID="gen28262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28263" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that he may--</hi>take me hence? No; that he dares not to ask.<div eID="gen28263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28264" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dip ... tongue--</hi>that is the least conceivable and the most momentary abatement of his torment; that is all. But even this he is told is (1) unreasonable. <div eID="gen28264" type="x-p"/>
entries.4141e051448dba58fd199b81e9fb533162d41734: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14619"/><div sID="gen28265" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14619"/><hi type="bold">25-26. Son--</hi>stinging acknowledgment of the claimed relationship.<div eID="gen28265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28266" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou ... Lazarus, &c.--</hi>As it is a great law of God's kingdom, that the nature of our present desires shall rule that of our future bliss, so by that law, he whose "good things," craved and enjoyed, were all bounded by time, could look for none after his connection with time had come to an end (<reference osisRef="Luke.6.24">Lu 6:24</reference>). But by this law, he whose "evil things," all crowded into the present life, drove him to seek, and find, consolation in a life beyond the grave, is by death released from all evil and ushered into unmixed and uninterrupted good (<reference osisRef="Luke.6.21">Lu 6:21</reference>). (<reference osisRef="2Cor.6.2">2</reference>) It is impossible. <div eID="gen28266" type="x-p"/>
entries.6e7ce0aba2fd9a05af75e84ba33e9dd3d8ae91d9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv14621"/><div sID="gen28269" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv14621"/><hi type="bold">27-31. Then he said--</hi>now abandoning all hope for himself.<div eID="gen28269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen28270" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">send him to my father's house, &c.--</hi>no waking up of good in the heart of the lost, but bitter reproach against God and the old economy, as not warning him sufficiently [Trench]. The answer of Abraham is, They are sufficiently warned. <div eID="gen28270" type="x-p"/>

entries.550fdd4579493d960ba890a9a75040500c4fb7c4: <div eID="gen40771" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen40772" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen40773" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen40773" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen40772" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen40774" type="x-p"/> The parable of the unjust steward, <reference osisRef="Luk.16.1-Luk.16.8">Luk 16:1-8</reference>. Christ applies this to his hearers, <reference osisRef="Luk.16.9-Luk.16.13">Luk 16:9-13</reference>. The Pharisees take offense, <reference osisRef="Luk.16.14">Luk 16:14</reference>. Our Lord reproves them, and shows the immutability of the law, <reference osisRef="Luk.16.15-Luk.16.17">Luk 16:15-17</reference>. Counsels against divorce, <reference osisRef="Luk.16.18">Luk 16:18</reference>. The story of the rich man and the beggar, commonly called Dives and Lazarus, <reference osisRef="Luk.16.19-Luk.16.31">Luk 16:19-31</reference>. <div eID="gen40774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40775" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen40775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40776" type="x-p"/> A steward - Οικονομος, from οικος, a house, or οικια, a family, and νεμω, I administer; one who superintends domestic concerns, and ministers to the support of the family, having the products of the field, business, etc., put into his hands for this very purpose. See on <reference osisRef="Luk.8.3">Luk 8:3</reference> (note). <div eID="gen40776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen40777" type="x-p"/> There is a parable very like this in Rab. Dav. Kimchi's comment on Isaiah, <reference osisRef="Isa.40.21">Isa 40:21</reference> : "The whole world may be considered as a house builded up: heaven is its roof; the stars its lamps; and the fruits of the earth, the table spread. The owner and builder of this house is the holy blessed God; and man is the steward, into whose hands all the business of the house is committed. If he considers in his heart that the master of the house is always over him, and keeps his eye upon his work; and if, in consequence, he act wisely, he shall find favor in the eyes of the master of the house: but if the master find wickedness in him, he will remove him, מן יפקדתו min pakidato, from his Stewardship.
