Cor. <ns0:hi>The word sig<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nifieth a mea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sure contain<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing fourteen bushels and a puttle.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> measures of wheat. And he said unto him, Take thy bill, and write fourscore.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 And the lord commended the unjust steward, because he had done wisely, for the children of this world are in their generation wiser then <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Eph. 5.8. 1 Thess. 5.5.</ns0:note> the chil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dren of light.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Hierom</ns0:hi> of old, thought this <ns0:hi>Parable</ns0:hi> was very obscure, and and <ns0:hi>Iulian</ns0:hi> and other <ns0:hi>Apostates,</ns0:hi> together with some of the <ns0:hi>Hea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />then Philosophers,</ns0:hi> took occasion from it to reproach the Do<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctrine of Christ, as teaching and commanding Acts of unrigh<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />teousness. But there will appear no such Difficulty in it, nor cause of Reproach to Christ, and his Doctrine from it, if we con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sider what I have before hinted: That it is no more necessary to a Parable, that all the Actions in it supposed be just and honest, than that all the parts of it be true in matter of Fact, whether past or possible to be, for a Parable is not designed to in<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>orm us in a matter of Fact, but to describe to us our Duty, under a Fictitious Representation: nor doth<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> every part of a Parable, point at some Correspondent duty to be done by us, but the main Scope for which it is brought, is principally to be attended by us, and other pieces of Duty which may be hinted in us, are to be judged of, and proved not from the Parable, but from other Texts of Holy Writ, where it is inculcated. The main things in which our Saviour seemeth desirous by this Parable to instruct us, are, 1. <ns0:hi>That we are but Stewards of the good things God lends us.</ns0:hi> and must give an account to our Master of them. 2. That being no more then <ns0:hi>Stewards</ns0:hi> intrusted with some of our Masters Goods for a time, it is our highest Prudence, while we have them in our Trust, to make such an use of them, as may be for our advantage, when we give up our Account. Thus we shall hear our Lord in the following Verses Expounding his own meaning. To this purpose he supposed a Rich Man to have a <ns0:hi>Steward,</ns0:hi> and to have received some Accusation against him, as if he imbezelled his Masters Goods Committed to his trust. Up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on which he calleth him to account, and tells him that he should be his Steward no longer. He supposeth this Steward be one who had no other means of Lively-hood, and subsistence, than what his Place afforded him, a Man not used to Labour, and too proud to Beg. At length he fixed his Resolution, to send for his Ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sters Debters, and to abate their Obligations, making them Deb<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ters to his Master for much less than indeed they were; by this means he probably Hoped, that when he was turned off from his Master, he should be received by them. He supposeth his Master to have heard of it, and to have commended him not for his Honesty, but for his Wit in providing for the time to come. What was Knavery in this Steward, is honest enough in those who are the <ns0:hi>Stewards</ns0:hi> of our <ns0:hi>Heavenly Lord</ns0:hi>'s <ns0:hi>Goods</ns0:hi>; suppose Riches, Honours, Parts, Health, Life, or any outward Accom<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />modation, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> to use our <ns0:hi>Lord</ns0:hi>'s <ns0:hi>Goods</ns0:hi> for the best profit, and advantage to our selves, during such time as we are instrusted with them. For tho an Earthly Lord, and his Steward, have particular divided Interests, and he that maketh use of his Lords Goods for his own best advantage, cannot at the same time make use of them for the best advantage of his Master, yet the Case is different betwixt our Heavenly Lord and us. It hath pleased God so to twist the Interest of his Glory with our highest good, that no Man can better use his Master's Goods for the advantage of his Glory, than he who best useth them for the highest good profit, and advantage to himself: Nor doth any Man better use them for his own Interest, than he who best useth them for Gods Glory. So as here the <ns0:hi>Parable</ns0:hi> halteth, by reason of the disparity betwixt the things that are compared. And tho the unjust Steward could not be commended for the honesty, but only for the Policy of his Action, yet we who are Stewards of the Gifts of God in doing the like, that is, making use of our <ns0:hi>Master</ns0:hi>'s <ns0:hi>Goods</ns0:hi> for our own best profit, and advantage, may Act not only wisely, but also honestly; and indeed Christ in this Parable blameth Men for not doing so. <ns0:hi>The Children of this World</ns0:hi> (saith he) <ns0:hi>are wiser in their Generation, than the Children of Light.</ns0:hi> By <ns0:hi>the Children of the World,</ns0:hi> he meaneth such as this Steward was, Men who regard not Eternity or the concerns of their immortal Souls, but only regard the things of this Life, what they shall Eat, or Drink, or put on. By the <ns0:hi>Children of the Light,</ns0:hi> he meaneth such a<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> live under the Light of the Gospel, and receive the common Illumination of the Gospel; tho if we yet understand it more strictly, of those who are <ns0:hi>Translated out of Darkness into marvellous Light,</ns0:hi> it is too true, they are not so Wise, and Politick, and Indu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />strious for Heaven, as Worldly Men are to obtain their ends in getting the World. He saith, <ns0:hi>The Men of the World are wi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ser in their Generation,</ns0:hi> that i<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, in <ns0:hi>their kind,</ns0:hi> as to those things, about which they Exercise their Wit, and Policy, than the Children of God.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 And I say unto you, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 6.19. <ns0:hi>&</ns0:hi> 19.21. 1 Tim. 6.17</ns0:note> Make to your selves friends of the <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>Riches.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> mammon of unrighteousness, that when ye fail, they may receive you into everlasting habitations.<ns0:note place="bottom">That by <ns0:hi>Mammon</ns0:hi> here is meant <ns0:hi>Riches,</ns0:hi> is universally a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />greed, but whether it Originally be a <ns0:hi>Chaldaick</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Syriack,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                           <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>nick</ns0:hi> Word is not so well agreed<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> The <ns0:hi>Chaldee Paraphrast,</ns0:hi> useth it, <ns0:hi>Hos.</ns0:hi> 5.11. But the <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> there is qu<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> otherwise, (ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cording to our Translation) <ns0:hi>They willingly <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                           <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>llowed the Com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mandment.</ns0:hi> But if the notion of those be <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, that some of those Nations had an <ns0:hi>Idol</ns0:hi> called <ns0:hi>Mammon,</ns0:hi> whom they made <ns0:hi>The God of Riches,</ns0:hi> answering the <ns0:hi>Grecian Plutus,</ns0:hi> it fairly interprets the <ns0:hi>Chaldee Paraphrast.</ns0:hi> They followed the com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mand for Idolatry, for such was <ns0:hi>Iereboam's</ns0:hi> Commandment, mentioned in that Text, and from thence it might be that the <ns0:hi>Syrians</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Punicks</ns0:hi> called <ns0:hi>Riches Mammon.</ns0:hi> We have the Word in the New Testament four times, thrice in this Chapter, on<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>e <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 6.24. It is called the <ns0:hi>Mammon of unrighteousness,</ns0:hi> by an <ns0:hi>Hebraism,</ns0:hi> it is as much as the <ns0:hi>unrighteous Mammon,</ns0:hi> by which we must not understand ill gotten Goods, (for <ns0:hi>God hat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth Robery for a Burnt Offering</ns0:hi>) we must restore such Goods, not make Friends of them: But Riches are so called, because of the Manifold Temptations to Sin, which arise from them, upon which account they are also called <ns0:hi>Deceitful.</ns0:hi> But others think that it is so called in opposition to the <ns0:hi>true Riches,</ns0:hi> mentioned <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 11. So that the <ns0:hi>Mammon of unrighteousness,</ns0:hi> is the <ns0:hi>Mammon</ns0:hi> of Falshood, or hurtful Riches, <ns0:hi>Riches of hurtfulness</ns0:hi> (<ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> sometimes signifies <ns0:hi>Hurt</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Wrong,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 
                     <ns0:hi>laedere, nocere.</ns0:hi>) Of these Riches, which are no true Riches, and which deceive the Soul, and do hurt, and mischief to a Soul, exposing it to Temp<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tation. Christ commands us to <ns0:hi>make Friends,</ns0:hi> either, 1. To make <ns0:hi>God our Friend,</ns0:hi> not by meriting from him any thing by our disposal of them, but by obedience to his Will in our distri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bution of them. 2. Or make poor Christians our Friends, so as we may have their Prayers. So that when <ns0:hi>ye fail,</ns0:hi> when you dye, when ye fail of any more comfort from them, <ns0:hi>they may receive you into everlasting Habitations.</ns0:hi> The Holy Trinity, or the blessed Angels (whose Work it is, as we shall hear) to carry Souls into <ns0:hi>Abraham's Bosom,</ns0:hi> may receive you into Heaven,</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:316" />10 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 19.17.</ns0:note> He that is faithful in that which is least, is faithful also in much, and he that is unjust in the least, is unjust also in much.<ns0:note place="bottom">This is an usual Sentence, (our Saviour made use of many such) as to which kind of Speeches it is not necessary they should be universally true, it is sufficient if they <ns0:hi>generally</ns0:hi> be so. Besides, that our Saviour plainly speaketh here according to the com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mon opinion, and judgment of Men. Men ordinarily judge that he who is faithful in a little thing, of no high concern or moment, will b<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> faithful in what is of an higher concern, or greater Moment, and if they have found a Person unfaithful in a small thing, they will conclude that he will be so in a greater, and not trust him; tho sometimes it falls out otherwise, that one who is faithful enough in some trifling things, prove unfaith<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ful in a greater trust, where unfaithfulness will turn more to his profit; and on the contrary, he that is unfaithful in a little thing, may prove more faithful in a greater, but none will trust to that, and that is our Saviours design, to teach us that God will do by us, as we in the like Case do by our Servants, or Neighbours.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 If therefore ye have not been faithful in the unrighteous mammon, who will commit to your trust the true <ns0:hi>riches</ns0:hi>?<ns0:note place="bottom">This Verse now opposeth the <ns0:hi>unrighteous Mammon</ns0:hi> to the <ns0:hi>true Riches,</ns0:hi> which would strongly incline one to think, that by the <ns0:hi>Mammon of unrighteousness</ns0:hi> before mentioned, our Sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />viour meant only false, and deceitful Riches. By the <ns0:hi>true Riches,</ns0:hi> I cannot think, is meant <ns0:hi>the Gospel,</ns0:hi> which indeed is said to be committed to trust of the Ministers, but not of all Christians. I had rather interpret it of <ns0:hi>special effectual Grace,</ns0:hi> which is of all other the true Riches, and so it teacheth us this great Truth. <ns0:hi>That God is justifyed, in the denial of his special Gra<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>e. to those who do not make a due use of his common Gifts and Grace,</ns0:hi> and indeed here will lie Mens Damnation, because they do not make a just use of that common Grace which they have, and might make a better use of them then they do. If they would be faithful in that, God would not deny them the <ns0:hi>true Ri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ches.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 And if ye have not been faithful in that which is another mans, who shall give you that which is your own?<ns0:note place="bottom">Let it be questioned whether <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> might not have been Translated <ns0:hi>Foreign</ns0:hi> as well as <ns0:hi>another Mans,</ns0:hi> for so Interpre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ters expound that Phrase. If you have not been faithful <ns0:hi>in things that are without you,</ns0:hi> which are little, compared with things that are within us. Yet <ns0:hi>Riches</ns0:hi> are indeed properly not ours, we are but the Stewards of them, and part of them are <ns0:hi>o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther Mens,</ns0:hi> and only trusted into our Hands, to dispense <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>o them according to our Masters order. <ns0:hi>Grace</ns0:hi> is our own, espe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cially justifying and sanctifying Grace<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> because it is given us of God solely for our own use and advantage. We use to say, <ns0:hi>That those who have been bad Servants, seldom prove good Masters.</ns0:hi> In the trust of our Riches, we are but Servants, God will not give out of his special saving Grace, to those that abuse the trust of his common Gifts and Grace.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 No servant can serve two masters: for ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other Ye cannot se<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="2 letters">
                     <ns0:desc>••</ns0:desc>
                  </ns0:gap>e God and mammon.<ns0:note place="bottom">See the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 6.24.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 And the Pharisees also <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 23.14.</ns0:note> who were covetous, heard all these things: and they derided him.<ns0:note place="bottom">Concerning the <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> Covetousness, we have often heard before, and indeed they were so from this Principle, that none but the Rich were happy, and blessed, and that all poor People were Cursed, <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 7.49. in opposition to whom some think that our Saviour, <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 6.20. Blessed the Poor. The promises relating to the old Testament, and made to the Jews, were generally of <ns0:hi>Temporal Blessings,</ns0:hi> tho under them Spiritual Mercies were also understood. As Hypocrites can never en<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dure to have their beloved Lusts touched, and Persons that have Drank in an Error, have no patience to hear it contradicted; so the <ns0:hi>Pharisees</ns0:hi> had no patience to hear that Doctrine, which crossed what they had taught, and struck at their darling Lusts. They <ns0:hi>derided him.</ns0:hi> The Word used, signifyeth a deriding with the highest degree of Scorn and Contempt.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 And he said unto them, Ye are they which justify your selves before men; but <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 7.9.</ns0:note> God know<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />eth your hearts: for <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Sam. 16.7.</ns0:note> that which is highly estee<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />med amongst men, is abomination in the sight of God.<ns0:note place="bottom">By justifying here is to be understood either an appearing be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore Men, as just, and strict observers of the Law, or 2. A predicating of themselves as just, you (saith our Saviour) make a fine shew, and great brags amongst Men: but Gods Eye goeth deeper, he knoweth the Heart; what Pride and Covetousness, and Hypocrisy lodgeth there. Men do not know your Hearts, <ns0:hi>but</ns0:hi> God knoweth them. <ns0:hi>All is not Gold</ns0:hi> by God's Touch<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stone, <ns0:hi>that Glistreth in Mans Eyes.</ns0:hi> Nay many things which are highly esteemed amongst Men, as matters of great Devoti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on and Piety and Merit, and which they applaud others for, are in the sight of God no better than <ns0:hi>Abominations.</ns0:hi> This highly obligeth all, not to make their estimate of things from the value, and Estimate which Men put upon them: Not e<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />very thing, but many things which are highly esteemed amongst Men are Abomination in the sight of God.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">16 The law and the prophets <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> until John, since that time the kingdom of God is preached, and every man presseth into it.<ns0:note place="bottom">We had the Sum of these Words, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 11, 12, 13. See the Notes on those Verses. The Connexion of these Words in this place seems to be this. Do no think it strange, that I Preach some Doctrines to you, which seem new to you, tho indeed they are no other then was before contained in the pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cepts of the old Testament, For the Law of the Prophets, the preaching of them, held but till <ns0:hi>Iohn,</ns0:hi> since whose time the Go<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spel hath been Preached, which gives you a clearer light into the Will of God, than you had before, and it pleaseth God to give it a great acceptation in the World, tho you reject it, <ns0:hi>every one presseth,</ns0:hi> that is, many press into it, so as God will not want a People, tho you mock and deride the Gospel instead of im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bracing of it, as you ought to do.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 102.26, 27. Isa. 40.8. & 51.6. Mat. 5.18.</ns0:note> And it is easier for heaven and earth to pass, then one tittle of the law to fail.<ns0:note place="bottom">Neither do you scandalize me, as if I came to teach a new Doctrine, contrary to the Law, and the Prophets. I tell you the quite contrary; Heaven and Earth shall pass away, before one tittle of the Law shall pass. Your vain interpretations of the Law, shall be destroyed, or amended, but the Law of my Fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther shall remain as a certain rule of Life, to his People, until the World shall have an end.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 7.10.</ns0:note> Whosoever putteth away his wife, and marrieth another, committeth adultery: and who<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />soever marrieth her that is put away from <ns0:hi>her</ns0:hi> hus<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />band, committeth adultery.<ns0:note place="bottom">See the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 5.32. where this is expounded, as also in the Notes on <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 19.9. <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 10.11.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="19">19 There was a certain rich man which was cloath<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed in purple, and fine linnen, and fared sumptuously every day.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="20">20 And there was a certain begger named Lazarus, which was laid at his gate, full of sores,</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">21 And desiring to be fed with the crumbs which <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                     <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                  </ns0:gap>ell from the rich mans table: moreover the dogs came and licked his sores.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 And it came to pass that the begger died, and was carried by the angels into Abrahams bosom: The rich man also died, and was buried.<ns0:note place="bottom">It is a Question of no great concern for us to be resolved about, whether this be an <ns0:hi>History,</ns0:hi> or Narrative of matter of Fact, or a <ns0:hi>Parable.</ns0:hi> Those that contend on either side have probable Argu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments for their Opinion, and it may be they best judge, who de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />termine it to be neither the one, nor the other, but a profitable discourse, that hath in it something of both. Our chief concern is to consider what our Lord by it designed to instruct us in. And certainly those do not judge amiss who think, that this discourse hath a great reference to what went before, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 9.10. where our Sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />viour had been exhorting his heares<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                     <ns0:hi>to make themselves Friends of the Mammon of Vnrighteousness,</ns0:hi> as also to the Pharisees de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />riding him for his Doctrine, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 14. Our Lord by this discourse letting them know the danger of <ns0:hi>Covetousness,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Vncharitable<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness,</ns0:hi> and also letting them know that <ns0:hi>what is highly esteemed amongst Men, may be abomination in the sight of God.</ns0:hi> He telleth them there was a certain rich Man, who lived in great <ns0:hi>Plenty</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Splendour,</ns0:hi> his clothing was <ns0:hi>Purple</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>fine linnen,</ns0:hi> that is exceeding costly, and splendid, his fare or Diet, was <ns0:hi>delicate</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Sumptuous,</ns0:hi> and that every day, from whence may easily be concluded, that if he had had an heart thereunto<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> he might have spared something for the Poor. Nor were the ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />jects of his charity far off. <ns0:hi>There was a certain Begger, whose name was Lazarus,</ns0:hi> poor enough, for he was full of sores, and would have been glad of the offal of the Rich Mans table; but the <ns0:hi>Dogs</ns0:hi> were more charitable then their Master; we read of nothing which the Rich Man gave him, but the <ns0:hi>Dogs</ns0:hi> came and licked his Sores. What was the end of this? The <ns0:hi>Begger</ns0:hi> died, and he was by the <ns0:hi>Angels carried into the bosom of Abraham,</ns0:hi> that is, into Heaven, some will have the Phrase signifie, one of the chiefest Mansions in Heaven. <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> was the Father of believers, and an hospitable Person while he lived upon the Earth. <ns0:hi>Lazarus</ns0:hi> is expressed to have been conveyed to him. There are many things discoursed by Men of Wit and Learning about this <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi>'s <ns0:hi>bosom,</ns0:hi> but the best <ns0:hi>center</ns0:hi> here, that by it is meant Heaven, and from hence two great points are proved. 1. <ns0:hi>That the Soul is capable of an existence separated from the Body,</ns0:hi> and therefore is not as some Atheists Dream, a meer affection of that, and an accident, but a distinct spiritual subsistence. 2. <ns0:hi>That the Souls of the Good, when they depart from their Bodies, imme<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />diately pass into an eternal state of Blessedness.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="23">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:316" />23 And in hell he lift up his eyes, being in torments, and seeth Abraham afar off, and Lazarus in his bo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />som.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24 And he cried and said, Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Zech. 14.12.</ns0:note> cool my tongue; for I <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 66.24. Mark 9.44. <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> am tormented in this flame.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 
                     <ns0:hi>and in Hell.</ns0:hi> The World hath been filled with disputes, about the true signification of the Word <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> which is here translated <ns0:hi>Hell.</ns0:hi> The most probably true notion of it is; that it signifies, <ns0:hi>the state of the Dead,</ns0:hi> both of the <ns0:hi>Dead Body,</ns0:hi> and so it often signifieth the <ns0:hi>Grave,</ns0:hi> and of the <ns0:hi>departed Soul.</ns0:hi> A very Learned Man saith, that if he mistaketh not, This is the only Test in Scripture, in which by it is to be understood, <ns0:hi>the place of Torments.</ns0:hi> The <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> Word which is translated by this, far more often signifying the place of the Blessed, whither the Saints and Patriarchs went when they Died, then the place whither Sinners went; but <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 24. makes it appear, that here it signifies <ns0:hi>Hell,</ns0:hi> properly so called, as it importeth the <ns0:hi>place of the Damned.</ns0:hi> We must understand our Saviour in this whole <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> to speak to us figuratively that by things which we understand, we might comprehend spiritual things. Heaven and Hell are at two great a distance, for Souls in each to discourse one with another; neither have Souls any Eyes to lift up. We are by this taught 1. That as the Souls of good Men when they leave their Bodies, go into an estate of eternal Bliss, where are <ns0:hi>Abraham, Isaac,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Iacob,</ns0:hi> and enjoy a felicity which we are not able to express, but is set out to us under the Notion of <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi>'s <ns0:hi>bosom,</ns0:hi> to let us know that it is a place of rest, and Communion with Saints, and the same felicity which <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> the Friend of God, doth enjoy: So the Souls of Wicked Men when they leave their Bodies, shall go into a place of <ns0:hi>Torments,</ns0:hi> the greatness of which being such as we are not able to conceive, they are expressed to us under the Notion of being <ns0:hi>tormented by Fire.</ns0:hi> 2. That it will be a great part of the misery of Damned Souls. To understand those to be in a state of happiness, whom they in this Life have scorned, de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spised, and abused, and it may be, have been instruments to hasten them to those Blessed Mansions. 3. That there will come a time when the Proudest Sinners, will be glad of the help of the meanest Saints, if they could obtain it. <ns0:hi>Father Abraham</ns0:hi> (saith the Rich Man) send <ns0:hi>Lazarus,</ns0:hi> that <ns0:hi>Lazarus</ns0:hi> whom when alive, I suffered to lye at my Gate full of Sores, and would not relieve. 4. That the state of the Damned will be void of the least degrees of Comfort and Satisfaction. The Rich Man desireth but a cooling of his Tongue, with so much Water, as could be brought upon the tip of <ns0:hi>Lazarus</ns0:hi> his finger. 5. <ns0:hi>That the Tongue is a Member, the abuse of which will in another Life, lye very heavy upon lost Souls.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">25 But Abraham said, Son, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Joh. 21.13.</ns0:note> remember that thou in thy life-time receivedst thy good things, and likewise Lazarus evil things: but now he is comfort<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed, and thou art tormented.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">26 And besides all this, between us and you there is a great gulf fixed: so that they which would pass from hence to you, cannot; neither can they pass to us, that <ns0:hi>would come</ns0:hi> from thence.<ns0:note place="bottom">We must still remember, that all these things are spoken in a Figure. The <ns0:hi>great Gulf</ns0:hi> here mentioned, to be fixed between Heaven and Hell, is to wide for Persons on opposite sides of it, to be heard communicating their Minds each to other. All that our Saviour designs to let us know, is, that the circumstances of Damne<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> Souls, are such, that if it were possible, they would beg the help and assistance of the meanest Saints, whom they have in this Life most scorned, despised, or abused, but as they will have no such opportunities as to crave any thing at their hands<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> so if they had, they could not receive the least relief from them, their state is determined, they are fixed for Eternity, and there can be no change of their condition for the better. <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> is here brought in calling this Man <ns0:hi>Son,</ns0:hi> either as lineally descended from him, or being a Member of that Church of which he was the Father. It will add to the Torments of the Damned, to hear and consider the former means, and advantages they have been under for Salvation, if they have descended from Godly Parents, or have been Members of the Church of Christ. <ns0:hi>That in thy Life-time thou receivedst thy good things, and likewise</ns0:hi> Lazarus <ns0:hi>evil.</ns0:hi> The <ns0:hi>good things</ns0:hi> which the Rich Man received, were no more the cause of his Damnation, than the <ns0:hi>evil things</ns0:hi>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> which <ns0:hi>Lazarus</ns0:hi> met with, were <ns0:hi>the cause of his Salvation,</ns0:hi> but the Rich Mans ill use of the former, and <ns0:hi>Lazarus</ns0:hi> his good <ns0:hi>improvement of the latter,</ns0:hi> through the Grace of God bestowed on him. Tho it be not ordinary with God, to give the same Persons the upper, and the nether Springs, yet he sometimes doth it, of which <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Lot,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Iob,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Isaac,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Iacob,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Ioseph</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>Arimathea,</ns0:hi> are some instances; but the term, <ns0:hi>thy,</ns0:hi> signifies the error of this Rich Man; he look't upon the good things of this Life as his portion, those were the things which he set his heart upon, and let his heart run out to the neglecting the good things of another Life. <ns0:hi>Lazarus</ns0:hi> received <ns0:hi>Evil things,</ns0:hi> God gave him a mean afflicted portion in this Life, but he was found patient, and glorifying of God by a quiet and believing submission to his Will under them, <ns0:hi>now he is comforted, and thou art tormented.</ns0:hi> So then it seemeth that departed Souls do not Sleep, as some have Dreamed, if they did they could neither have been capable of Comfort or Torment. <ns0:hi>And besides all this, there is a great Gulf fixed,</ns0:hi> &c. the meaning of which is no more then, 1. <ns0:hi>That the state of Souls upon their separation from the Bodies of Men and Women, is determined and fixed.</ns0:hi> As the tree falls, so it lyeth: 2. That there is no Commerce or Intercourse, betwixt Glorified and Damned Souls. The <ns0:hi>Papists</ns0:hi> passage from <ns0:hi>Purgatory</ns0:hi> to Heaven, is a new found way, or rather a new fancyed one; if <ns0:hi>Purgatory</ns0:hi> be (as they pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tend) a place where Souls <ns0:hi>are tormented,</ns0:hi> it may be admired how they should pass over this Gulf: it seemeth <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> did not know the way, Saint <ns0:hi>Peter</ns0:hi> knew as little; this is one of his <ns0:hi>pretended Vicars</ns0:hi> new discoveries, but it is no Wisdom in any Souls to trust to this passage, of which <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> knew as little, as he did of our Prayers passing to them, or to God for them, for there is <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. <ns0:hi>A great Gulf established.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">27 Then he said, I pray thee therefore, father, that thou wouldest send him to my fathers house.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="28">28 For I have five brethren; that he may testifie unto them, lest they also come into this place of tor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment.<ns0:note place="bottom">Him, that the Rich Man would not hear, when he lay at his Gate full of Sores, exhorting him <ns0:hi>to do good, and to distribute, to give Alms of all that he had, and to make himself Friends of the Mammon of Vnrighteousness,</ns0:hi> he would now have restored to the Earth again, his Soul before the general Resurrection re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />united to his Body, that he might go unto his Fathers house, and give them warning, that they might not come into the misery which he felt. <ns0:hi>But is there any charity in Hell</ns0:hi>? Is there any there, that wish well to Souls upon Earth; or rather are not Damned Souls, like Persons infected with the Plague, desirous that others might be made as miserable as themselves. A Grave and Acute Author saith, he Prayeth not for them, but for himself, that he might not be the more miserable, by the company of those who upon the Earth were his near Relations, and dear unto him. But we must remember that our Saviour here speaketh all in a Figure, and that which our Saviour by these expressions designeth to instruct us in, is no more than this. That altho Atheistical, and Proud and haughty Souls in this Life, make a mock at Hell, and at the wrath of God to be revealed after this Life, and despise the poor Servants of God, who by their Doctrine, or holy Life, and example would teach them better things, yet they shall find the fire of Hell so hot, the Wrath of God so terrible, and intolerable, that if you could imagine, that Souls under those Miseries, could have the least Dramm of Charity, and good Nature left in them, tho they apprehend themselves past all hopes, or recovery to a better state, yet they would beg that some of those faithful Ministers, or Godly People, whom they have rejected. despised, and abused, might be sent to every Friend they have in the World, to warn them from doing as they have done, and running the hazard of those <ns0:hi>Tor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments</ns0:hi> they feel for doing of such things. The <ns0:hi>Papists</ns0:hi> who idly go about from hence to prove, a sense in <ns0:hi>departed Souls of the state of their Friends</ns0:hi> that are yet alive upon the Earth, can derive very lit<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tle comfort from that speculation out of this Text; which if it could prove any thing of that Nature, could prove no more, then that <ns0:hi>Damned Souls have such a sense,</ns0:hi> and might by the same Argu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment also evince their Charity. But figurative expressions must not be so tente<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="3 letters">
                        <ns0:desc>•••</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>. I have shewed what I judge to be the true instruction from this passage.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="29">29 Abraham saith unto him, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 8.20.34.16. Act. 15.21.17.11.</ns0:note> They have Moses and the prophets<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> let them hear them.<ns0:note place="bottom">Christ here representeth to us the Genius of Wicked and Carnal Men, that would be converted by Revelations and some extraordi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nary Signs, if they could see one <ns0:hi>risen from the Dead,</ns0:hi> then they would <ns0:hi>believe the Resurrection,</ns0:hi> if they could see a Glorified Saint, or hear or see a Damned Soul, then they would believe an <ns0:hi>Heaven</ns0:hi> and an <ns0:hi>Hell</ns0:hi>: he here brings in <ns0:hi>Abraham</ns0:hi> saying<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                     <ns0:hi>They have</ns0:hi> Moses <ns0:hi>and the Prophets, l<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>t them hear them.</ns0:hi> God will have Men believe the propositions of his Word, and live up to the rule of Life, prescribed there, and not expect to have their curiosity satisfied, by needless and extraordinary Revelations. But is there then no need of the Gospel to bring Men to Heaven, doubtless there is, but that is included in <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Prophets,</ns0:hi> who all Prophecied of Christ, tho more darkly then he is revealed in the New Testament. <ns0:hi>Had ye believed</ns0:hi> Moses, <ns0:hi>ye would have believed me, for he wrote of me, Iohn</ns0:hi> 5.46 <ns0:hi>& v.</ns0:hi> 39. <ns0:hi>search the Scriptures, for in them ye think that you have eternal Life, and they testifie of me</ns0:hi>: now they at that time, had no Scriptures to search, but those of <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Prophets</ns0:hi>; for the New Testa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment was not at that time Written.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="30">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:317" />30 And he said, Nay, father Abraham: but if one went unto them from the dead, they will repent.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="31">31 And he said unto him, If they hear not Moses and the prophets, neither will they be perswaded though one rose from the dead.<ns0:note place="bottom">How vain is Man in his imaginations? We are prone all of us, to think after the rate, that this <ns0:hi>Rich Man</ns0:hi> is here brought in speaking. That altho Persons be Deaf to the sound of the Word, yet some sensible evidence of the Wrath of God, would make a change in their hearts and lives. There is no such thing. There is not possibly in all the Book of God, a Text that more speaks the desperate <ns0:hi>hardness</ns0:hi> of a Sinners heart, then this, nor a Text, which looks more dreadfully upon Persons siting under the means of Grace, reading and hearing the Word of God, and yet find not their hearts so affected with the reading, and hearing of it, as there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />by to be brought to repentance, and Faith, and such Holiness of Life as it requireth. If it were possible that such Men and Women should see one come out of the bottomless Pit, tearing his hair, and wringing his hands, and gnashing his teeth, and bewailing his Misery, and begging of them to be wise by his example, telling them for what Sins he is made so miserable, and with tears and highest expressions of Passion, beseeching them that while they have time, they would leave of those courses, <ns0:hi>acquaint them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves with God, and be at Peace, that thereby good might come unto them,</ns0:hi> they would not yet believe nor Repent, nor would this have any further effect upon them, then a little Passion, till they could get the Din out of their Ears. For tho sensible evidence, be the highest advantage in the World to moral suasion; yet these things are under no Divine appointment to such an effect. Hence<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />forth let us wonder no more that a <ns0:hi>Drunkard</ns0:hi> sees his Companion drop down Dead before him, yet presently cries again, <ns0:hi>fill the Glass,</ns0:hi> that hundred of Sinners are daily hurried down to Hell in their Wickedness, and yet their Companions take no warning. In a fight at Sea or Land hundreds drop, yet their Companions do not fly, but are held up by their Stomachs, and Passion, and their Ears are made deaf by the noise of the Drums and Trumpets. So in the World hundreds of Sinners drop down daily into the Pit, yet the rest of their Companions, tumble their Companions into their Graves, and never consider the work of the Lord, nor con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sider the operation of his hands, till they also like Sheep be laid in the Grave, and Death comes to feed upon them, and Hell to de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vour them also. This now to those that duly con<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ider not things, and in particular do not consider this Text, seemeth strange and amazing. But it is no more to be wondred at, then that hundreds read, and hear the Word of God, and are not by it Converted and Changed. It is not to be expected that any Providence of God, should work upon those Souls any salvifick change, upon whom the Word doth not work. That is the ordinance of God with which the holy Spirit joyns it self, which alone can produce this change. If God works not this change, he will work it by nothing else. Tho he sometimes maketh use of such Providences towards Souls to whom he intendeth good, to make them observe, and attend to the Word better, in order to so Blessed an effect.</ns0:note>
